Hölder’s Inequality

This scene widens Cauchy–Schwarz to general exponents. The key is that the two exponents come as a matched pair.

Multiply two sequences term by term and add them up: even that total has a ceiling. The ceiling is the product of the two sequences' norms. With both exponents equal to 2, it is exactly Cauchy–Schwarz. The key step is Young's inequality, which trades a product for shares of a sum. The precise formulas are below.

For example, at a 🏪 shop you multiply each item's price by its quantity and add everything up. That total never exceeds the product of the price list's size and the quantity list's size.

∑k=1n∣akbk∣≤(∑k=1n∣ak∣p)1/p(∑k=1n∣bk∣q)1/q\sum_{k=1}^{n} |a_k b_k| \le \left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} |a_k|^p\right)^{1/p} \left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} |b_k|^q\right)^{1/q}k=1∑n​∣ak​bk​∣≤(k=1∑n​∣ak​∣p)1/p(k=1∑n​∣bk​∣q)1/q
ab≤app+bqq(Young)ab \le \frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^q}{q} \quad \text{(Young)}ab≤pap​+qbq​(Young)

Applying the monotone exp⁡\expexp to both sides, exp⁡(1plog⁡(ap)+1qlog⁡(bq))=ab≤app+bqq\exp\left(\frac{1}{p}\log(a^p) + \frac{1}{q}\log(b^q)\right) = ab \le \frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^q}{q}exp(p1​log(ap)+q1​log(bq))=ab≤pap​+qbq​ — Young's inequality proved.

    Verify the zero cases directly as well: if a=0a = 0a=0 then the left side is ab=0ab = 0ab=0 and the inequality reads 0≤bqq0 \le \frac{b^q}{q}0≤qbq​, with equality only when bq=0b^q = 0bq=0, i.e. b=0b = 0b=0 — exactly what ap=bqa^p = b^qap=bq (namely 0=bq0 = b^q0=bq) asserts; the case b=0b = 0b=0 is symmetric.

    This equality condition becomes Hölder's equality case in problem 3 below.

Prove the exact equality condition in Hölder's inequality: equality holds if and only if either ∥a∥p∥b∥q=0\|a\|_p \|b\|_q = 0∥a∥p​∥b∥q​=0 (one of a,ba, ba,b is the zero sequence, so both sides are 000), or there exists a constant C>0C > 0C>0 with ∣ak∣p=C ∣bk∣q|a_k|^p = C\,|b_k|^q∣ak​∣p=C∣bk​∣q for all kkk.

equality  ⟺  [∥a∥p∥b∥q=0] or [∃ C>0: ∣ak∣p=C ∣bk∣q ∀k]\text{equality} \iff \Big[\|a\|_p \|b\|_q = 0\Big] \ \text{or}\ \Big[\exists\, C > 0:\ |a_k|^p = C\,|b_k|^q \ \forall k\Big]equality⟺[∥a∥p​∥b∥q​=0] or [∃C>0: ∣ak​∣p=C∣bk​∣q ∀k]
Show proof

  1. Separate the degenerate case first.

    If ∥a∥p∥b∥q=0\|a\|_p \|b\|_q = 0∥a∥p​∥b∥q​=0 then one of a,ba, ba,b is the zero sequence, so ∑∣akbk∣=0\sum |a_k b_k| = 0∑∣ak​bk​∣=0 and the right side is also 000 — equality holds automatically.

    Note: with b=0b = 0b=0 but a≠0a \ne 0a=0, this equality holds, yet no constant — not even C≥0C \ge 0C≥0, let alone C>0C > 0C>0 — satisfies ∣ak∣p=C∣bk∣q|a_k|^p = C|b_k|^q∣ak​∣p=C∣bk​∣q (the right side is identically 0 while some ∣ak∣p>0|a_k|^p > 0∣ak​∣p>0).

    That is why the first branch of the statement is indispensable.

    In both directions below, the degenerate case is settled by this paragraph, and the proportional branch is treated under ∥a∥p,∥b∥q>0\|a\|_p, \|b\|_q > 0∥a∥p​,∥b∥q​>0.

  2. (⇒)(\Rightarrow)(⇒) Assume ∥a∥p,∥b∥q>0\|a\|_p, \|b\|_q > 0∥a∥p​,∥b∥q​>0 and that equality holds overall.

    In problem 2's proof the inequality happened in exactly one place: Young's inequality AkBk≤Akpp+BkqqA_k B_k \le \frac{A_k^p}{p} + \frac{B_k^q}{q}Ak​Bk​≤pAkp​​+qBkq​​ applied to each term.

    Equality gives ∑kAkBk=1\sum_k A_k B_k = 1∑k​Ak​Bk​=1, while ∑k(Akpp+Bkqq)=1p∑Akp+1q∑Bkq=1\sum_k \left(\frac{A_k^p}{p} + \frac{B_k^q}{q}\right) = \frac{1}{p}\sum A_k^p + \frac{1}{q}\sum B_k^q = 1∑k​(pAkp​​+qBkq​​)=p1​∑Akp​+q1​∑Bkq​=1 is an identity, so if any single term were strict, the summed inequality would be strict — hence equality holds for every kkk.

    By problem 1's equality condition, Akp=BkqA_k^p = B_k^qAkp​=Bkq​ for every kkk; unwinding the normalization gives ∣ak∣p∥a∥pp=∣bk∣q∥b∥qq\frac{|a_k|^p}{\|a\|_p^p} = \frac{|b_k|^q}{\|b\|_q^q}∥a∥pp​∣ak​∣p​=∥b∥qq​∣bk​∣q​ — i.e. ∣ak∣p=C∣bk∣q|a_k|^p = C|b_k|^q∣ak​∣p=C∣bk​∣q with C=∥a∥pp/∥b∥qq>0C = \|a\|_p^p/\|b\|_q^q > 0C=∥a∥pp​/∥b∥qq​>0 (both norms are positive) independent of kkk.

  3. (⇐)(\Leftarrow)(⇐) Conversely, assume one of the two branches.

    If the degenerate branch ∥a∥p∥b∥q=0\|a\|_p \|b\|_q = 0∥a∥p​∥b∥q​=0 holds, the first paragraph already verified equality with both sides 000 — this also covers the C=0C = 0C=0 case: if ∣ak∣p=0⋅∣bk∣q|a_k|^p = 0 \cdot |b_k|^q∣ak​∣p=0⋅∣bk​∣q for all kkk, then a=0a = 0a=0 and the first branch applies with no division by any norm.

    For the proportional branch, assume ∣ak∣p=C∣bk∣q|a_k|^p = C|b_k|^q∣ak​∣p=C∣bk​∣q for all kkk and some C>0C > 0C>0.

    If ∥b∥q=0\|b\|_q = 0∥b∥q​=0 then b=0b = 0b=0 and proportionality forces a=0a = 0a=0 as well, returning to the degenerate branch; if ∥a∥p=0\|a\|_p = 0∥a∥p​=0 then a=0a = 0a=0, again the degenerate branch.

    In the remaining case ∥a∥p,∥b∥q>0\|a\|_p, \|b\|_q > 0∥a∥p​,∥b∥q​>0, division by the norms is legitimate: summing the proportionality over kkk forces C=∥a∥pp/∥b∥qqC = \|a\|_p^p/\|b\|_q^qC=∥a∥pp​/∥b∥qq​, and after normalization Akp=∣ak∣p∥a∥pp=∣bk∣q∥b∥qq=BkqA_k^p = \frac{|a_k|^p}{\|a\|_p^p} = \frac{|b_k|^q}{\|b\|_q^q} = B_k^qAkp​=∥a∥pp​∣ak​∣p​=∥b∥qq​∣bk​∣q​=Bkq​, so by problem 1's equality condition every Young's inequality is an equality: AkBk=Akpp+BkqqA_k B_k = \frac{A_k^p}{p} + \frac{B_k^q}{q}Ak​Bk​=pAkp​​+qBkq​​.

    Summing over kkk gives ∑kAkBk=1p∑kAkp+1q∑kBkq=1p+1q=1\sum_k A_k B_k = \frac{1}{p}\sum_k A_k^p + \frac{1}{q}\sum_k B_k^q = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} = 1∑k​Ak​Bk​=p1​∑k​Akp​+q1​∑k​Bkq​=p1​+q1​=1, i.e. ∑k∣akbk∣=∥a∥p∥b∥q\sum_k |a_k b_k| = \|a\|_p \|b\|_q∑k​∣ak​bk​∣=∥a∥p​∥b∥q​ — equality in Hölder's inequality.

  4. In the scene, ak=1/ka_k = 1/kak​=1/k and bk=1b_k = 1bk​=1 have both norms positive but ∣ak∣p|a_k|^p∣ak​∣p is not constant, so the gap can never be 0 — the gap closing as p→1+p \to 1^+p→1+ is a collapse of the right side itself, not proportionality.
